title: kubelet and containerd in endless loop for CreateContainer with unexpected media type octet-stream
body:
### What happened?

I think the private container registry had some intermittent errors and did return wrong data for some layers.

The problem I think is that kubelet or containerd is in a state were it assumes that a given OCI image is already downloaded locally, but then some parsing of this layer fails and the loop starts again.

### What did you expect to happen?

kubelet and or containerd should detect the wrong layer/manifest state and delete the incomplete/erroneous download and pull again from container registry.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Not sure, probably container registry needs to return media type octet-stream for some layer/manifest instead of correct media type.

The error message I see in the logs are probably come from here:
https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.7.15/images/image.go#L238
Not sure about exact containerd version but I think it's 1.7.x

In the pod events we see thousands of events like:
"Container image "xyz" already present on machine" Pulled.
This seems to originate from here:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/v1.28.7/pkg/kubelet/images/image_manager.go#L138

So kubelet thinks that image is already present and successful pulled, but then containerd fails with:
"failed to create containerd container: error unpacking image: unexpected media type application/octet-stream for sha:xyz: not found: CreateContainerError"

The containerd fails probably here:
https://github.com/containerd/containerd/blob/v1.7.10/images/image.go#L238

Looks like something with the local manifest bookkeeping is not correct, which hinders container creation.

Maybe containerd can detect that image layer/manifest is read from local cache and remove erroneous cached local image layers
/sig node

> kubelet and or containerd should detect the wrong layer/manifest state and delete the incomplete/erroneous download and pull again from container registry.

containerd should identiffy the corrupt layer and remove it, that's nothing the kubelet should do. The kubelet only tells the runtime to pull images when they're not present on disk.

Do you mind moving that issue to the containerd repo?
opened in containerd as https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/10136

I know it's an old issue, but I hit the same issue on a "flacky registry" - turns out it's caused by a combination of fallback behaviour of containerd https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/13007 plus how certain registry handles `GET /blobs` and `HEAD /blobs` requests.

> I know it's an old issue, but I hit the same issue on a "flacky registry" - turns out it's caused by a combination of fallback behaviour of containerd [containerd/containerd#13007](https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/13007) plus how certain registry handles `GET /blobs` and `HEAD /blobs` requests.

So this will be fixed by fixing containerd or anything else is needed from k8s?

Yes, the issue can be fixed on containerd and CNCF distribution side

https://github.com/containerd/containerd/issues/13007
https://github.com/distribution/distribution/issues/4812

I don't think anything is needed on k8s side.

title: The APIServer health check failed. As a result, the APIServer automatically exits and APIServer unavailable.
body:
### What happened?

Most services access the APIServer through the service of the ClusterIP type. The relationship between the service and the endpoints is created by the APIServer , and then the iptables routing rule maintained by kube-proxy. When the APIServer is restarted, the routing rule cannot be updated quickly. A large amount of service traffic is received. CPU resources are limited and the CPU usage is high. As a result, the APIServer health check timeout and then the APIServer exits automatically. As a result, the service is unavailable.

### What did you expect to happen?

Before the APIServer is started successfully, a filter is added to the ingress to control the incoming traffic, ensuring that the APIServer can be started successfully and enhancing the APIServer reliability.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

When the APIServer is started, a large number of requests are sent to the APIServer. As a result, the CPU is overloaded and the APIServer health check times out.

title: --hostname-override flag on kubelet is no longer used for Addresses.Hostname value in Kubernetes 1.29
body:
### What happened?

It looks like there was a change that first appeared in Kubernetes 1.29, where in 1.29 the `--hostname-override` flag on kubelet is no longer being used to populate the Node's Addresses.Hostname value.  Here is the relevant output from a `kubectl describe node` for a 1.28 cluster with `hostname-override=10.X.X.X`:

```
Addresses:
  InternalIP:  10.X.X.X
  ExternalIP:  52.X.X.X
  Hostname:    10.X.X.X
```

And here's the output from a 1.29 cluster with the same configuration:

```
Addresses:
  InternalIP:  10.X.X.X
  ExternalIP:  52.X.X.X
```

Here is the full `kubelet` list of parameters in case that is helpful:

`/usr/local/bin/kubelet --config=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet-config.yaml --root-dir=/var/data/kubelet --node-labels=privateVLAN=XXXXXXX,publicVLAN=XXXXXXX --cloud-provider=external --v=2 --kubeconfig=/etc/kubernetes/kubelet-kubeconfig --hostname-override=10.X.X.X --enable-controller-attach-detach=false --version=v1.28.9+IKS --runtime-cgroups=/podruntime/runtime`

This is from an IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service 1.28 and 1.29 cluster.  We do not think there was any cloud-configuration-manager or any other related change that would cause this difference.  Is it possible it is a side effect of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/121028 ?

### What did you expect to happen?

I expected the behavior to be consistent between Kubernetes releases, since I didn't find any reference to this change in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/CHANGELOG/CHANGELOG-1.29.md

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Create an IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service cluster at 1.28 and 1.29 and see the difference

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

No, it's just a dumb kubelet startup bug. Well, not dumb, but easy to fix.

It seems the problem is that once kubelet sets the hostname the cloud controller manager does not override it


https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/da479a82ebb6d4117b69f2c78364c81a513ad511/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L373-L388

so maybe the right behavior is only override it if is actually overridden ?

> It seems the problem

what problem?

> It seems you are relaying on the node.status.address with type Hostname and this not clearly documented
> 
> [#126099 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/126099#discussion_r1677991212)

(Well, to clarify my comments there: it's not well-defined _between different clouds and node linux distros_. If you know what cloud and distro you are on, then the behavior might be consistent and usable, but that still makes for a lousy kubernetes API.)

Anyway, the question here is: was this actually breaking anything major, or did you just happen to notice this and think "that's weird"?

(Also, if anyone else was broken by this bug, feel free to chime in; trying to figure out what to do about backporting this, because the original fix for this bug ended up introducing another bug, and the fix for _that_ bug is maybe not backport-able...)

So far I have only heard from a single customer (who was using IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service) who had something in their cluster relying on cluster node's Address.Hostname value, and so when they updated to 1.29 they were broken.  I believe they just modified their code to get this "Hostname" value (which was really the node IP) from somewhere else.

So, to answer the question, it is somewhere between the "I noticed it and thought 'that's weird'" option and the "it broke something major" option.   We have this documented in our 1.29 release notes for IBM Cloud Kubernetes Service, so other customers will have fair warning before updating.  So at this point I don't consider fixing this in 1.29 as essential.

nodes.title: Fix behavior with external cloud provider and --hostname-override
nodes.body:
#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug
/kind regression

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
#121028 changed kubelet startup to not try to autodetect the node IP when using an external cloud provider, but accidentally also changed it to not write out the kubelet-provided hostname value.

Pre-121028, the `if !nodeIPSpecified { return nil }` wasn't there, so it ended up adding an autodetected node IP and the hostname [below](https://github.com/danwinship/kubernetes/blob/4da16d5c07d82267ada50eca20504a93856a8272/pkg/kubelet/nodestatus/setters.go#L233-L236) (whether that hostname was autodetected or overridden). This patch just revises that so we always add the hostname like before, we just don't write out the nodeIP if it wasn't user-specified.

(The 2 unit tests that this changes the behavior of are the 2 that were added in #121028.)

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #124453

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
The logic here can be simplified once we drop the legacy cloud provider case, but (a) I wasn't sure what that was waiting for, and (b) this patch needs to be backported anyway.

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
Fixed a regression where `kubelet --hostname-override` no longer worked
correctly with an external cloud provider.
```

/cc @aojea

title: CVE-2024-3177: Bypassing mountable secrets policy imposed by the ServiceAccount admission plugin
body:
CVSS Rating: [CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N](https://www.first.org/cvss/calculator/3.1#CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:H/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N) - **Low** (2.7)

A security issue was discovered in Kubernetes where users may be able to launch containers that bypass the mountable secrets policy enforced by the ServiceAccount admission plugin when using containers, init containers, and ephemeral containers with the envFrom field populated. The policy ensures pods running with a service account may only reference secrets specified in the service account’s secrets field. Kubernetes clusters are only affected if the ServiceAccount admission plugin and the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation are used together with containers, init containers, and ephemeral containers with the envFrom field populated. 

### Am I vulnerable?

The ServiceAccount admission plugin is used. Most cluster should have this on by default as recommended in  https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/admission-controllers/#serviceaccount
The kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets annotation is used by a service account. This annotation is not added by default. Pods using containers, init containers, and ephemeral containers with the envFrom field populated.

#### Affected Versions

kube-apiserver v1.29.0 - v1.29.3
kube-apiserver v1.28.0 - v1.28.8
kube-apiserver <= v1.27.12

### How do I mitigate this vulnerability?

This issue can be mitigated by applying the patch provided for the kube-apiserver component. The patch prevents containers, init containers, and ephemeral containers with the envFrom field populated from bypassing the mountable secrets policy enforced by the ServiceAccount admission plugin.

Outside of applying the provided patch, there are no known mitigations to this vulnerability.

#### Fixed Versions

- kube-apiserver master - fixed by #124322
- kube-apiserver v1.29.4 - fixed by #124325
- kube-apiserver v1.28.9 - fixed by #124326
- kube-apiserver v1.27.13 - fixed by #124327

To upgrade, refer to the documentation:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/administer-cluster/cluster-upgrade/ 

### Detection

Pod update requests using a container, init container, or ephemeral container with the envFrom field populated that exploits this vulnerability with unintended secret will be captured in API audit logs. You can also use the following kubectl command to find active pods using the `kubernetes.io/enforce-mountable-secrets` annotation. 

`kubectl get serviceaccounts --all-namespaces -o jsonpath="{range .items[?(@.metadata.annotations['kubernetes\.io/enforce-mountable-secrets']=='true')]}{.metadata.namespace}{'\t'}{.metadata.name}{'\n'}{end}"` 

If you find evidence that this vulnerability has been exploited, please contact security@kubernetes.io

#### Acknowledgements

This vulnerability was reported by tha3e1vl. 

The issue was fixed and coordinated by the fix team: 

Rita Zhang @ritazh
Joel Smith @joelsmith
Mo Khan @enj

and release managers:
Sascha Grunert @saschagrunert
Jeremy Rickard @jeremyrickard

/kind bug

title: Pod soft evicted is still ready in kubernetes 1.24+ .
body:
### What happened?

If pod was soft evicted, it will keep ready until all container dead. Endpoints of the pod will not be removed.

When kubelet triggers soft eviction, the status manager will try to report the phase as failed.
And there are still running containers, the phase of newStatus will be overwritten by oldStatus.

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9791f0d1f39f3f1e0796add7833c1059325d5098/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1097-L1103

And then status manager will calculate pod condition by phase of oldStatus.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/9791f0d1f39f3f1e0796add7833c1059325d5098/pkg/kubelet/status/status_manager.go#L1109-L1117

This will lead to pod still ready, and the endpoint will not be removed until the container is killed, even if the Prestop Hook has been executed.

### What did you expect to happen?

Kubelet will mark pod as not ready, if eviction triggered.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Start kubelet with args `--eviction-soft-grace-period=allocatableMemory.available=10s --eviction-soft=allocatableMemory.available<2Gi`
2. Create a pod and handle SIGTERM.
3. Run stress in pod cgroup.
4. Run `for c in `seq 1 1000`; do kubectl get pod -o yaml <pod-name> > `date +%T`.yaml; sleep 1; done

We'll see pod still ready until failed.

### Anything else we need to know?

From https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/117822.

### Kubernetes version

v1.26.1 or v1.28.3

### Cloud provider

No matter.

### OS version

No matter.

### Install tools

No matter.

### Container runtime (CRI) and version (if applicable)

No matter.

### Related plugins (CNI, CSI, ...) and versions (if applicable)

No matter.

After experiements, I find that it might be caused by the image name. 

If we export and import image with only version (or digest) like:
```
sudo ctr images export dashboard-0.45.0.tar gcr.io/tekton-releases/github.com/tektoncd/dashboard/cmd/dashboard:v0.45.0
```
and run in kubernetes use same tag, it works.
```
kubectl run tekton-dashboard-test --image=gcr.io/tekton-releases/github.com/tektoncd/dashboard/cmd/dashboard:v0.45.0 --image-pull-policy=Never
```

however, if we use version and digest at sametime, it does not work:

```
gcr.io/tekton-releases/github.com/tektoncd/dashboard/cmd/dashboard:v0.45.0@sha256:5cd17db16f6b930e85d051a5669b032e5680ec80c2c87bc3a2f0134d55a53c38
```

it seems that kubernetes is finding image with digest if it's provided, in the above case, kubernetes is looking for `gcr.io/tekton-releases/github.com/tektoncd/dashboard/cmd/dashboard@sha256:5cd17db16f6b930e85d051a5669b032e5680ec80c2c87bc3a2f0134d55a53c38` 

instead of `gcr.io/tekton-releases/github.com/tektoncd/dashboard/cmd/dashboard:v0.45.0@sha256:5cd17db16f6b930e85d051a5669b032e5680ec80c2c87bc3a2f0134d55a53c38`

I'm not sure if it's correct.

I wonder if this really belongs in containerd.

@mikebrow should we move this to containerd?

`:tag@digest` generally really just means `@digest`, the tag is for humans only.

you can test this with e.g. `docker pull $image:fake-tag@real-digest`
yeah, it seems that this is by design. I'll close it.

title: kube-scheduler: pod stuck in `PENDING` but added to active queue
body:
### What happened?

We are writing a scheduler plugin using the scheduling framework. However, when creating a pod that uses out secondary scheduler e.g. by using

```
schedulerName: my-scheduler
```

The scheduler logs:
```
I0411 14:59:41.249623       1 eventhandlers.go:126] "Add event for unscheduled pod" pod="ns/pod1"
I0411 14:59:41.249678       1 scheduling_queue.go:575] "Pod moved to an internal scheduling queue" pod="ns/pod1" event="PodAdd" queue="Active"
```

but then nothing happens. The pod is stuck in `PENDING` state. Also, no events are created. 
We have the same scheduler running against a k8s v1.29 EKS cluster fine. It appears the pod is never retrieved from the active queue, e.g. [this line](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/pkg/scheduler/schedule_one.go#L68) is never hit.

### What did you expect to happen?

The pod should get scheduled or fail unscheduled.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Build a scheduler plugin using versions below and run on k8s v1.21.14.

### Anything else we need to know?

Versions from `go.mod`:
<details>

```console

title: Broken connectivity while using IPVS, ExternalIP and externalTrafficPolicy: Local
body:
### What happened?

First of all, I read the related issues (https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kubespray/issues/10572, https://github.com/k3s-io/k3s/issues/7183, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121272, https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/117613) and realized that the problem is still exists in mainstream.

I'm dealing with a Kubernetes cluster managed by Kubespray. It's set up in IPVS mode and uses Calico as a CNI. The cluster is tightly coupled with our network infrastructure: it announces all the types of Kubernetes IPs into ToR switches via BGP (so called IP Fabric Network Design).

In this scheme, the simplest way to assign a globally routed IP into a Service is to declare an ExternalIP. This doesn't require to interact with any kind of Kubernetes API using third-party software (like LoadBalancerIP do), Calico simply catches up the IPs like this and informs the switches about. That's why I can't consider ExternalIPs as an ancient concept (https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/121272#issuecomment-1770986681), they simplify the things.

All the ExternalIPs are automatically assigned to kube-ipvs0 which is great and all work fine with "externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster". But if I change the policy to Local, connections from outside a Kubernetes node to the corresponding ExternalIP become broken with "icmp-port-unreachable" error caused by iptables:

```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-HEALTH-CHECK-NODE-PORT dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
```

### What did you expect to happen?

It seems the only thing that the externalTrafficPolicy does in the network stack is moving ExternalIPs between KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP and KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP-LOCAL ipsets, but there's no equivalent RETURN rule for the -LOCAL one in the iptables. If I insert the rule manually:

```
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-EXTERNAL-IP-LOCAL dst,dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m set --match-set KUBE-HEALTH-CHECK-NODE-PORT dst -j RETURN
-A KUBE-IPVS-FILTER -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -m set --match-set KUBE-IPVS-IPS dst -j REJECT --reject-with icmp-port-unreachable
```
"externalTrafficPolicy: Local" works as expected. BTW, I have no idea why we should reject anything here at all, do you?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Deploy a single node with IPVS mode. Declare a Service with ExternalIP and externalTrafficPolicy: Local. See the ExternalIP works locally, but filtered from outside the node.

title: exec probe should kill timeout process
body:
### What happened?

The process of exec probe may enter the `S` state due to some reasons. If it still does not end after the timeout period, the process will not exit, and more and more processes will accumulate, resulting in consuming a large amount of resources.

### What did you expect to happen?

kill timeout process

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

Make a probe that doesn't quit like this

```yaml
        readinessProbe:
          exec:
            command:
            - sh
            - -c
            - sleep 10000
          # It's just a simulation of processes that don't exit, the reality can be a bit more complicated
          initialDelaySeconds: 5
          periodSeconds: 5
          timeoutSeconds: 1
```

### Anything else we need to know?

Notice this warning in the [k8s docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#configure-probes)

But why don't we kill this process by kubelet after timeout? What is the reason for keeping it?


> Caution: Incorrect implementation of readiness probes may result in an ever growing number of processes in the container, and resource starvation if this is left unchecked.

here we are immediately closing the connection after successful connect leading to EOF at server end (it is expecting data) causing the failure.
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22140b6a070e09589b5b2bcdf5c396114f25274f/test/images/agnhost/connect/connect.go#L116-L122


We can tweak this to connect send some data just like UDP and then exit?
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/22140b6a070e09589b5b2bcdf5c396114f25274f/test/images/agnhost/connect/connect.go#L55

Works locally writing "hostname" to the connection.

[EDIT]

For me it sometimes failed with EOF, sometime with nil pointer exception at `conn.RemoteAddr().String()`.
https://github.com/ishidawataru/sctp/blob/master/sctp.go#L602 This reads sock opts via syscall and we immediately close the connection .. kind of a race between the client closing connection and server reading fds?

the panic seems a bug in that project, no?
Also SCTP, has a establishment handshake, so the data should not be relevant in this case

[Accept(4)](https://linux.die.net/man/2/accept4) returns fd and socket address, for [TCP the returned socket address](https://github.com/golang/go/blob/master/src/internal/poll/sock_cloexec_accept.go#L22) is used to implement `RemoteAddr` (always read from struct field).

The SCTP implementation discards the returned socket address by `Accept` call.
https://github.com/ishidawataru/sctp/blob/7ff4192f6ff2b4b181ec7dce269bdf4076ff90a0/sctp_linux.go#L235, and `RemoteAddr` is always a new syscall ([SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/sctp.7.html#:~:text=passed%20to%20users.-,SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS,-This%20option%20is)). 

In our case the client immediately closes the connection, there can be chances where SCTP_GET_PEER_ADDRS will fail and `RemoteAddr` will return nil in these cases.  I think this is reasonable for their project. 

We call `conn.RemoteAddr().String()` and panic is raised by calling `String()` on nil object. We can easily avoid this by not null check. Also, I strongly believe that the client handling should be done in a separate go-routine instead of the main loop to avoid errors like this crashing the pod.

[EDIT]

The client in our case needs to send some data after connection, or else the server will throw EOF and we currently have assertions that use `log.Fatal` for errors.

>  I think this is reasonable for their project.

panicing does not seem very reasonable

It looks to me that the problem is that the SCTPConn struct needs to check if the connection is still valid before trying to access the file descriptor , see the std library implementation https://github.com/golang/go/blob/5c20d5faeb3d048a31896f3edfb54dbd960d07cc/src/net/net.go#L173

and then, all methods implement this check 

https://github.com/golang/go/blob/5c20d5faeb3d048a31896f3edfb54dbd960d07cc/src/net/net.go#L226-L230

to me it is a bug on the implementation

> panicing does not seem very reasonable

The implementation is not causing any panic, it simply returns nil. 
```go
conn.RemoteAddr() -> nil
```
Panic is caused when we try to call `.String()` on nil object.
```go
conn.RemoteAddr().String() 
```

oh, sorry, my bad I should read your comment with more detail, is well explained there

I recognize I have zero idea of how sctp works internally, maybe we can just be more resilient on our tests and code and detect if is nil and avoid getting into the complexity of this protocol ... sending some random data also sounds good, we do this for udp IIRC
@aroradaman are you able to send a PR to add those improvements to the test image?

fine, I found the key point.
`hack/_update-generated-protobuf-dockerized.sh` shell will use `_output/bin/go-to-protobuf` first. So if you have a go-to-protobuf bin with older version, you will meet this error. 

You should remove older go-to-protobuf bin in `_output/bin` directory, and re-run `make update`

```
hack/_update-generated-protobuf-dockerized.sh content:

PATH="${KUBE_ROOT}/_output/bin:${PATH}" \
  go-to-protobuf \
  -v "${KUBE_VERBOSE}" \
  --go-header-file "${KUBE_ROOT}/hack/boilerplate/boilerplate.generatego.txt" \
  --output-dir="${KUBE_ROOT}/staging/src" \
  --proto-import="${KUBE_ROOT}/staging/src" \
  --proto-import="${KUBE_ROOT}/vendor" `# required for gogo.proto` \
  --proto-import="${KUBE_ROOT}/third_party/protobuf" \
  --packages="$(IFS=, ; echo "$*")"
```

title: BestEffort pods are using swap
body:
### What happened? I was testing the support for swap and I came to an unexpected behavior. In the documentation it is specified that only pods that fall under the `Burstable` class can use the host's swap memory. However, I created both a deployment with 1 replica of ubuntu belonging to the `Burstable` class, and one belonging to the `BestEffort` class, where I ran the command `stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 6G --vm-hang 0` to see the consumption of memory made. The host has 4GB RAM memory and 5GB swap. In both situations, the pod started using swap after exceeding the RAM memory requirement. Wasn't the BestEffort pod supposed to be restarted when it reached the limit of the host's RAM memory? I mention that the kubelet is configured to `swapBehavior=LimitedSwap`. I attached two pictures where you can see the normal consumption of host, and consumption after running stress command inside pod . ![screenshot_2024-03-27_at_12 37 02](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/26438926/1d60c115-46a5-4a4d-9aba-0c34a6411775) ### What did you expect to happen? I expected the `BestEffort` pod to be killed when it consumes more RAM memory than the host have available. ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)? - setup a VM running ubuntu 22.04 with 4GB of RAM memory - set swap partition to 5GB - install docker, cri-dockerd and kubernetes packages using the provided versions - config kubelet with provided config - install calico cni - after the cluster is bootstrapped, deploy the following deployment
```console $ $ cat test.yaml apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ubuntu-deployment labels: app: ubuntu spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ubuntu template: metadata: labels: app: ubuntu spec: containers: - name: ubuntu image: ubuntu:22.04 resources: command: [ "/bin/bash", "-c", "--" ] args: [ "while true; do sleep 30; done;" ] ```
- this should deploy a BestEffort pod. you can check this by running `kubectl get pod --output=yaml` - exec into the pod and do `apt update & apt install stress`. Then run `stress --vm 1 --vm-bytes 6G --vm-hang 0` - check the node where the pod is running with `kubectl get po -o wide` then ssh to that node and run `htop`. Now you should see that the deployed BestEffort pod is consuming swap memory, which according to the Docs, it shouldn't. - if exec into the pod and check `memory.swap.max`, this is set to max. From what I understand, even if `swapBehavior` was set to `LimitedSwap` in `kubelet`, somehow cri-dockerd may be set the cgroup for `memory.swap.max` to `max`.
```console $ cat /sys/fs/cgroup/memory.swap.max max ```
### Anything else we need to know? I am using cgroup v2. Here is my kubelet config.
```console $ cat /var/lib/kubelet/config.yaml apiVersion: kubelet.config.k8s.io/v1beta1 authentication: anonymous: enabled: false webhook: cacheTTL: 0s enabled: true x509: clientCAFile: /etc/kubernetes/pki/ca.crt authorization: mode: Webhook webhook: cacheAuthorizedTTL: 0s cacheUnauthorizedTTL: 0s cgroupDriver: systemd clusterDNS: - 10.96.0.10 clusterDomain: cluster.local containerRuntimeEndpoint: "" cpuManagerReconcilePeriod: 0s enableServer: true evictionPressureTransitionPeriod: 0s failSwapOn: false featureGates: NodeSwap: true fileCheckFrequency: 0s healthzBindAddress: 127.0.0.1 healthzPort: 10248 httpCheckFrequency: 0s imageMaximumGCAge: 0s imageMinimumGCAge: 0s kind: KubeletConfiguration logging: flushFrequency: 0 options: json: infoBufferSize: "0" verbosity: 0 memorySwap: swapBehavior: LimitedSwap nodeStatusReportFrequency: 0s nodeStatusUpdateFrequency: 0s resolvConf: /run/systemd/resolve/resolv.conf rotateCertificates: true runtimeRequestTimeout: 0s shutdownGracePeriod: 0s shutdownGracePeriodCriticalPods: 0s staticPodPath: /etc/kubernetes/manifests streamingConnectionIdleTimeout: 0s syncFrequency: 0s volumeStatsAggPeriod: 0s ```
### Kubernetes version
```console $ kubectl version Client Version: v1.29.3 Kustomize Version: v5.0.4-0.20230601165947-6ce0bf390ce3 Server Version: v1.29.3 ```
### Cloud provider
Hetzner Cloud, but Kubernetes was deployed using `kubeadm`.
### OS version
```console $ cat /etc/os-release PRETTY_NAME="Ubuntu 22.04.4 LTS" NAME="Ubuntu" VERSION_ID="22.04" VERSION="22.04.4 LTS (Jammy Jellyfish)" VERSION_CODENAME=jammy ID=ubuntu ID_LIKE=debian HOME_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/" SUPPORT_URL="https://help.ubuntu.com/" BUG_REPORT_URL="https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/" PRIVACY_POLICY_URL="https://www.ubuntu.com/legal/terms-and-policies/privacy-policy" UBUNTU_CODENAME=jammy $ uname -a Linux fs-kube-dev-1 5.15.0-100-generic #110-Ubuntu SMP Wed Feb 7 13:27:48 UTC 2024 x86_64 x86_64 x86_64 GNU/Linux ```
### Install tools
```console $ kubeadm version kubeadm version: &version.Info{Major:"1", Minor:"29", GitVersion:"v1.29.3", GitCommit:"6813625b7cd706db5bc7388921be03071e1a492d", GitTreeState:"clean", BuildDate:"2024-03-15T00:06:16Z", GoVersion:"go1.21.8", Compiler:"gc", Platform:"linux/amd64"} ```

Can you explain exactly what you expect to happen? is not very clear from your description,

do you expect that a pod that tries to connect to the Service ClusterIP `10.43.0.10` ends connected to the IP `10.0.0.5` ?

~Have you verified all connectivity works without services too?~

@PMacho assuming you are using kube-proxy, can you please paste an `iptables-save` from one of the worker nodes ?

@aojea 


The documentation of "Services without Selectors" https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#service-no-selector-access explicitly states 
> Accessing a Service without a selector works the same as if it had a selector. In the [example](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#services-without-selectors) for a Service without a selector, traffic is routed to one of the two endpoints defined in the EndpointSlice manifest: a TCP connection to 10.1.2.3 or 10.4.5.6, on port 9376.

Where the "example" defines:

``` yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-service
spec:
  ports:
    - protocol: TCP
      port: 80
      targetPort: 9376
```

and 
``` yaml
apiVersion: discovery.k8s.io/v1
kind: EndpointSlice
metadata:
  name: my-service-1 # by convention, use the name of the Service
                     # as a prefix for the name of the EndpointSlice
  labels:
    # You should set the "kubernetes.io/service-name" label.
    # Set its value to match the name of the Service
    kubernetes.io/service-name: my-service
addressType: IPv4
ports:
  - name: '' # empty because port 9376 is not assigned as a well-known
             # port (by IANA)
    appProtocol: http
    protocol: TCP
    port: 9376
endpoints:
  - addresses:
      - "10.4.5.6"
  - addresses:
      - "10.1.2.3"
```

Therefore, in my configuration I expect `r2dbc:mariadb://mariadb` to be routed to `10.0.0.5`, instead of complaining `Connection refused: mariadb.debug-endpoints.svc.cluster.local/10.43.202.125:3306`.

For the record, defining the service to be headless, i.e. `spec.clusterIP: "None"`, does route to `10.0.0.5`. However, https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/service/#headless-services states: 
> Sometimes you don't need load-balancing and a single Service IP.
Considering that the Database may very well be a cluster, this does not necessarily apply.


The requested output of `iptables save`, with the above configuration deployed to namespace `debug-endpoints`:
[iptables-save.txt](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/files/14624940/iptables-save.txt)

I'm in my way to kubecon so no much time until the week after, but this is a good issue for networking contributors to help, it seems pretty simple to reproduce as you are already providing the steps ... once reproduced is a matter of understanding why the kube-proxy does not see those EndpointSlices

@aroradaman @uablrek you are quite familiar with the proxy code, maybe you can take a look?

@PMacho I see you are defining ports with a name in the endpointslice but without a name in the service which is breaking our internal mapping of service to endpoints. 

Making both the ports either named or un-named should solve the issue. 

quick fix:
```
kubectl patch service mariadb --type='json' -p='[{"op": "add", "path": "/spec/ports/0/name", "value": "mysql"}]'
```
Maybe the docs could use a tweak to recommend setting a name for port 80?

yes, will update the doc.

/sig network
/assign @uablrek

I have a few questions:

> However, It looks possible that accessing specific service objects from outside of cluster. (e.g. accessing nginx NodePort service object, accessing ClusterIP service object via portforwarding)

So, from inside the cluster (i.e. from a node or pod), you can't access a service by it's domain name (DN), like:
```
<svc-name>.<namespace-name>.svc.cluster.local:<port>
```
but you can access the `clusterIP` of that service?

So, it's only the DNS query that doesn't work?

The resolv.conf listed is from a node, not a POD, and as I see it, it doesn't query the local "CoreDNS" in the cluster, which is the only one that knows about the .svc.cluster.local domain. So it's natural that the lookup fails.

The
```
UDP  10.96.0.10:53 rr
  -> 10.244.169.6:53              Masq    1      0          0         
  -> 10.244.240.215:53            Masq    1      0          0
```
is most likely the service for CoreDNS. So, inside a POD the resolv.conf should use `nameserver 10.96.0.10`.

Can you please verify this?

Also, if you install proxy-mode=ipvs from start, i.e. not proxy-mode=iptables, and then switch, does DNS from pods work?

I have tested this in [KinD](https://kind.sigs.k8s.io/) with K8s v1.29.1, and DNS lookup works. Both when proxy-mode=ipvs is configured from start, and when proxy-mode=iptables is configured and the configmap is altered to "ipvs", and kube-proxy instances are re-started.

/triage not-reproducible

#### Some observations

On the K8s _nodes_ `resolv.conf` looks like this:
```
# cat /etc/resolv.conf
# Generated by Docker Engine.
# This file can be edited; Docker Engine will not make further changes once it
# has been modified.

nameserver 172.18.0.1
search lan
options ndots:0

# Based on host file: '/etc/resolv.conf' (internal resolver)
# ExtServers: [192.168.10.1 fdc3:c0c4:458a::1]
# Overrides: []
# Option ndots from: internal
```
And DNS queries to `.cluster.local` does _not_ work (and shouldn't work):
```
# curl --insecure https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
curl: (6) Could not resolve host: kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
```

But from within a POD, it works:
```
# kubectl create namespace test-pod
# cat | kubectl create -n test-pod -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: test-pod
spec:
  containers:
  - name: alpine
    image: alpine
    command: ["sleep", "infinity"]
EOF
# kubectl exec -n test-pod test-pod -- cat /etc/resolv.conf
search test-pod.svc.cluster.local svc.cluster.local cluster.local lan
nameserver 10.96.0.10
options ndots:5
# kubectl exec -n test-pod test-pod -- wget https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local
Connecting to kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local (10.96.0.1:443)
481B7D4AAE740000:error:0A000086:SSL routines:tls_post_process_server_certificate:certificate verify failed:ssl/statem/statem_clnt.c:1889:
ssl_client: SSL_connect
wget: error getting response: Connection reset by peer
command terminated with exit code 1
```
The lookup to `kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` succeeds, but ssl authorization fails (which is expected).

@Ryu0n can you please provide more information?
For instance how `/etc/resolv.conf` looks in the POD where the lookup fails. And whenever the failing POD has "hostNetwork:true".
And, if possible, run "nslookup ..." inside that POD.

Your CoreDNS and the dns service seem OK, from what I can see in your "ipvsadm" dump. But you may check the logs for the CoreDNS pods.

Since this problem can't be reproduced, and no new information is provided, I close the issue.

/ close

Please reopen it if problem persist, and new info is available. If possible a way to reproduce it in KinD.
/close

title: Code generator is no longer usable via `go run`
body:
### What happened?

The code generator was usable via `go run` up until v1.30.0-alpha.3:

```console
$ go version
go version go1.22.1 linux/amd64
```

```console
$ go run k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/client-gen@v0.30.0-alpha.3 --help
Usage of /tmp/go-build2845286753/b001/exe/client-gen:
[...]
```

Since v1.30.0-beta.0:

```console
$ go run k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/client-gen@v0.30.0-beta.0 --help
go: k8s.io/code-generator/cmd/client-gen@v0.30.0-beta.0 (in k8s.io/code-generator@v0.30.0-beta.0):
        The go.mod file for the module providing named packages contains one or
        more replace directives. It must not contain directives that would cause
        it to be interpreted differently than if it were the main module.
```

### What did you expect to happen?

The code generator works via `go run`.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

See above.

### Anything else we need to know?

This may not be a supported way to use the code generator at all, but it worked quite well until now, and I thought I'd bring this to attention. IIUC the offending replace directive came in as part of the workspace support (#123529) and I'm not sure there's anything that can be done about it.

### Kubernetes version

<details>

```console
$ kubectl version
# v1.30.0-beta.0
```

N/A

title: readiness prober timeout do not run as expected
body:
### What happened?

1. We meet the issue that the readiness probe timeout do not run as expected.  It run as 2mins + timeout setting in actual 

2. According  to the below official kubernets doc, it define that the timeoutSeconds: Number of seconds after which the probe times out. Defaults to 1 second. Minimum value is 1.  After I read this infromation from the doc , i think it means if the prober command running time exceeded the timeout period, the kubelet will stop this prober action and start the next prober, butl it not in actual.  The next prober action  will run after the last prober  action completed or last prober action lasted (2mins + timeout setting).

https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/configure-pod-container/configure-liveness-readiness-startup-probes/#define-readiness-probes

3. I also check the code, and find that it deifine timeous =timeout setting  + default timeout (2 minutes) as timeout to leave some time for  the runtime to do cleanup uless timeout setting is 0s. I think 2 minutes is used for the containerd runtime to prepare necessary action. But the doc description make the customer confusion easily if not add  some details
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d1a2a134c532109540025c990697a6900c2e62fc/pkg/kubelet/cri/remote/remote_runtime.go#L469
![image](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/assets/88937681/3a53ef8c-e01a-40c9-8582-65c56feabb88)




### What did you expect to happen?

Could you plz modify the deafult timeout in code  or add description in  the officail doc ?

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. create a configmap  like below. it show the two commd: 1. create a file named with the current time; 2.  sleep 300s
```
apiVersion: v1
data:
  container-readiness-probe-handler.sh: |-
    #!/bin/sh
    touch /tmp/$(date +'%Y-%m-%d-%H-%M-%S')
    sleep 300
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: tesh

The timeout code you linked to is the timeout on the CRI call the to the runtime, not the actual timeout on the probe exec call. That should be the timeout specified in the ExecSync request here: 

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/d1a2a134c532109540025c990697a6900c2e62fc/pkg/kubelet/cri/remote/remote_runtime.go#L487-L493

If the longer timeout is being hit, that likely indicates a problem with the runtime, e.g. it timed out creating the exec process, or making the request. What version of containerd are you running?

I wasn't able to reproduce this with a quick check:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name:   probe-timeout
spec:
  volumes:
    - name: probe-log
      emptyDir: {}
  containers:
    - name:  alpine
      image: alpine:latest
      args: [sh, -c, 'while true; do sleep 100000; done']
      readinessProbe:      
        failureThreshold: 3
        periodSeconds: 10
        successThreshold: 1
        timeoutSeconds: 5
        exec:
          command: ['sh', '-c', 'date >> /probe/readiness-log.txt && sleep 300']
      volumeMounts:
        - mountPath: /probe
          name: probe-log
```
Output
```
$ kubectl exec -t probe-timeout -- tail -f /probe/readiness-log.txt

Thu Mar 14 21:02:09 UTC 2024
```

Note that the interval is sometimes 5s, and sometimes 10s. The 10s interval comes from the probe period, but the 5s is probably from retries on probe error. I'm not sure why it's inconsistent.

In either case, this sounds like it's probably a containerd issue, not a Kubernetes issue.

title: kube-proxy does not appear to be creating iptables entries

### What happened?

When setting up a new cluster using Kubernetes 1.29.2 on Debian 12.5 ("bookworm"), it appears that the necessary iptables entries to permit access to services, etc., are not being created by kube-proxy. body:
### What happened?

The `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6
```
--bind-address=aaaa:bbbb::2e8

```
The metrics port of kube-proxy listens to the ipv4 address
​```
netstat -nlap|grep 10249
tcp        0      0 127.0.0.1:10249         0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      5412/kube-proxy

### What did you expect to happen?

When the `--bind-address` parameter of kube-proxy is configured as ipv6, the ip address of metrics listens to ::1 by default

Thank you for this. 

Please use `--metrics-bind-address` flag to change metric listening address, docs are here: https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/command-line-tools-reference/kube-proxy/

as for the `--bind-address`, the docs are a bit confusing wrt to this field.

/kind support

--metrics-bind-address          ipport     Default: 127.0.0.1:10249
  | The IP address and port for the metrics server to serve on, defaulting to "127.0.0.1:10249" (if --bind-address is unset or IPv4), or "[::1]:10249" (if --bind-address is IPv6).

Set metrics-bind-address to ::1, the effect is as follows：
tcp6       0      0 ::1:10249               :::*                    LISTEN      30567/kube-proxy 

So the document can also be updated. --bind-address may  not be useful.
/triage accepted

title: Parallel pod deletion makes kubectl stuck forever
body:
### What happened?

`kubectl delete pod` may become stuck during execution of the following steps:
* Restart kubelet `systemctl restart kubelet`
* Force remove all containers for static pods `crictl ps --name '(kube-apiserver|kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd)' -q | xargs -I CONTAINER sudo crictl rm -f CONTAINER`
* Try to delete some static pod `kubectl delete pod -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-k8s-control-plane-1`

Result: kubectl prints that the pod is deleted, but never exits.

It seems that the problem is caused by parallel deletion of the pod by kubelet.
Please see details in the steps to reproduce.


### What did you expect to happen?

kubectl exits.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

1. Install single-node cluster
2. Run script
<details>

```sh
#!/bin/bash

for i in {1..100} ; do
  echo "Attempt $i"
  systemctl restart kubelet
  crictl ps --name '(kube-apiserver|kube-scheduler|kube-controller-manager|etcd)' -q | xargs -I CONTAINER sudo crictl rm -f CONTAINER
  for component in kube-apiserver kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager etcd; do
    while true ; do
      echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S,%N') delete $component"
      if kubectl --v=10 delete pod -n kube-system ${component}-k8s-control-plane-1 2> failed.txt ; then
        break
      fi
    done
  done
  for component in kube-apiserver kube-scheduler kube-controller-manager etcd; do
    while true ; do
      echo "$(date '+%H:%M:%S,%N') get $component"
      if kubectl get pod -n kube-system ${component}-k8s-control-plane-1 | grep '1/1' ; then
        break
      fi
      sleep 5
    done
  done
done
```
</details>

> Try to delete some static pod kubectl delete pod -n kube-system kube-controller-manager-k8s-control-plane-1

note that these are mirror pods, which serve more of an ~informal~ representative purpose. deleting them will tell the kubelet to re-create them at API level, but this delete action doesn't have much value.

> It seems that the problem is caused by parallel deletion of the pod by kubelet.

your test could be triggering some corner case around static pod sync.
as long as regular pods (non-mirror) can be deleted fine in parallel, without exhibiting this problem, then maybe this could be claimed as a problem around static pods and a "won't fix".

leaving this to sig node for triage, though. maybe there is a race that should be avoided.
/sig node

if you really want to delete these pods and stop the related containers, you should move/remove the YAML files in /etc/kubernetes/manifests.

This was a first attempt to do not really delete the pods and containers, but restart the containers and make sure they are restarted and ready. Without pod deletion, immediate attempt to check the pods might show an outdated status. Finally, other solution was developed avoiding the pod deletion.
cc: @smarterclayton
cc: @harche

I'm not sure this problem was completely caused by static pod deletions. I'd suggest repeat the steps for static pods that are *not* k8s control plane to isolate the problem to see if it still exists.

/triage needs-information
/priority backlog

Since we're using static pods here, I would recommend you delete the static pod manifests and let the kubelet take care of deleting the pods. I find the pattern of going behind its back to delete with crictl first odd and would recommend against it.

I need to restart the container, bot do not delete the static pod manifest. Restart is done through crictl. Pod deletion was supposed to refresh the readiness status to wait for (after it is created back automatically). Other ways to restart the container by updating or delete & create the manifest seem approximately the same weird, but I would appreciate if you could officially recommend something.

> delete & create the manifest seem approximately the same weird

I hear you. Often static pod files are managed by some controller or operator so this kind of manual intervention isn't needed. If you'd prefer to manage the lifecycle of the pod, maybe a non static pod would be better. But for static pod management, the most idiomatic way to restart or delete it is to change or delete the manifest AFAIU
Ok, please close the issue if decide to won't fix
/close

@pohly: The label(s) `sig/apimachinery` cannot be applied, because the repository doesn't have them.

<details>

In response to [this](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123172#issuecomment-1932065075):

>/sig apimachinery


Instructions for interacting with me using PR comments are available [here](https://git.k8s.io/community/contributors/guide/pull-requests.md).  If you have questions or suggestions related to my behavior, please file an issue against the [kubernetes/test-infra](https://github.com/kubernetes/test-infra/issues/new?title=Prow%20issue:) repository.
</details>
/sig api-machinery

Took a peek at this.

Looks like `Unregister` writes to `exposedPaths` under a lock:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/04aa8f9dcdbc575fde37e25e45315359b0aa1ca6/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/mux/pathrecorder.go#L151-L167


But `ListPaths` copies from it without a lock:

https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/04aa8f9dcdbc575fde37e25e45315359b0aa1ca6/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/server/mux/pathrecorder.go#L97-L103

This code is pretty old, I'm surprised we haen't caught this before

Well, We need a lock here..., I will file a fix for it.

/assign
/triage accepted

title: K8s can't live without a default route
body:
### What happened?

Derived from https://github.com/projectcalico/calico/issues/8481

I use a virtual cluster with router VMs. When I start without any router VM, no default route is setup on the K8s nodes. This makes load-balancing to services to fail, at least with proxy-mode=iptables/nftables, and just about all CNI-plugins to fail. In short, the cluster is dead.

With proxy-mode=ipvs service routing works, but there are more subtle problems, e.g. Calico doesn't start. I haven't investigated further.

### What did you expect to happen?

Well, to me it seems OK to _require_ a default route, but the problem must be documented somewhere where cluster admins will see it.

I can't really see any use-case where a default route is not set. Maybe when K8s is only used for SW-management, or security reasons.

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a test cluster:
1. curl -k https://kluster-svc-address
2. ip ro delete default
3. curl -k https://kluster-svc-address

For instance on KinD:
```
root@default-control-plane:/# curl -k https://10.96.0.1
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:anonymous\" cannot get path \"/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}root@default-control-plane:/# ip ro del default
root@default-control-plane:/# curl -k https://10.96.0.1
curl: (7) Couldn't connect to server
root@default-control-plane:/# 
```


### Anything else we need to know?

IMO this is a documentation issue.

> to me it seems OK to require a default route, but the problem must be documented somewhere where cluster admins will see it.

@sftim

I don't think this has anything to do with the default route, but actually, a route is needed on the host to allow access to service packets to be accepted by netfilter.

Before the packet arrives in the PREROUTING chain, there is a routing judgment there, and if the destination is found to be unreachable (similar to `ip r get <dst_ip>`), the packet will be dropped.

```
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗ curl -k https://10.233.0.1:443
curl: (7) Couldn't connect to server
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗ ip r get 10.233.0.1
RTNETLINK answers: Network is unreachable
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗ ip r add 10.233.0.1 dev eth0
➜  test git:(e687fb89) ✗ curl -k https://10.233.0.1:443
{
  "kind": "Status",
  "apiVersion": "v1",
  "metadata": {},
  "status": "Failure",
  "message": "forbidden: User \"system:anonymous\" cannot get path \"/\"",
  "reason": "Forbidden",
  "details": {},
  "code": 403
}#
```

ipvs is working properly because the host's kube-ipvs0 interface is configured with the address of the service, so it allows the packets accessing the service to arrive at the PREROUING chain and then passes them to the IPVS program on the INPUT chain for processing.

Good observation. Any route that matches the ClusterIP range will do it seems. I tested on KinD:
```
ip ro del default
ip ro add 10.96.0.0/16 dev lo
curl -k https://10.96.0.1  # (works)
```
But then externalIP's will not be routed, and since they are hard to predict, I think a default route really is a requirement.

```
ip ro add default dev lo
```
works :smile: And should be good enough for security, since stray packets will be discarded as [martians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martian_packet)
Yeah, we may need to document that the default route is a basic requirement, and most of the time we don't create special routes for the service.

hmm, we may need to document that nodes need IPs to communicate too :) 

People may want to use custom routes and this still work, I don't think we should make this a requirements, is a network design of the cluster and is not kubernetes the one to define this
But the custom route must be to the ClusterIP CIDR, of which a network admin would not be aware.

> But the custom route must be to the ClusterIP CIDR, of which a network admin would not be aware.

this is an installation and routing problem, why should not be aware of that?

in addition, there are deployments that use multihoming on nodes, one interface facing the internet and other interface for internal routing, and the ServiceCIDR should be routed through the internal interface for their services to work.

What I'm trying to point out is that one thing is the cluster setup and installation, that is a responsibility of cluster-api, kubeadm, kube-spray, home made scripts ... and these are the responsibles of designing the cluster and its routing, and other thing is the behavior of the components, those are different things.

> Well, to me it seems OK to require a default route, but the problem must be documented somewhere where cluster admins will see it.

related:
https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/create-cluster-kubeadm/#network-setup

>> Note: If the host does not have a default gateway and if a custom IP address is not passed to a Kubernetes component, the component may exit with an error.

same page recommends to have a default route vs passing custom IPs to all components.

> same page recommends to have a default route vs passing custom IPs to all components.

It's a bit worse actually. If you _don't_ have a default route, but you _do_ pass a custom IPs to all components, the installation with `kubeadm` will work (according to the docs), but K8s will not.

My point is that k8s should not mandate on how cluster should be implemented, just define the architecture and best practices, but asserting that k8s can not live without a default route is not true, is complex to setup but is feasible, and in depending how much complex scenarios, is sometimes required

So, an acceptable best practice recommendation would be something like:

> Unless the K8s nodes have a default route for the base family of the K8s cluster, a specific route has to be specified for the ClusterIP CIDR.

or something like "when setting up your cluster, you must ensure that your nodes are able to forward packets to the Service CIDR, this is commonly done by defining a default route, but in more complex network setups you must want to set it explicitly"
What are we going to do with this issue? It sounds like we are going to update documentation?
Yes, that's my proposal. But we can also just ignore it since no default route is rare. I can only think of security reasons.

The thing that breaks without a default route is load-balancing with `kube-proxy` (replacements may work). That in itself may not be a big deal since K8s doesn't _require_ load-balancing afaik, and other K8s components works, but...

Many crucial components, like CNI-plugins, assume that the "kubernetes" service can be used to access the API-server.

I can explain why it doesn't work, and what routes that must be setup if a default route doesn't exist, but this should be done in `kube-proxy` documentation rather than generic K8s. Then the kubeadm documentation can cross-reference to it.

@danwinship Is there documentation for `kube-proxy` that can be extended, and referred from kubeadm documentation?

> K8s doesn't _require_ load-balancing afaik, and other K8s components works, but...

it does require, Services is part of Conformance

> I can explain why it doesn't work, and what routes that must be setup if a default route doesn't exist, but this should be done in kube-proxy documentation rather than generic K8s

I just think the opposite, it should be great addition to the generic documentations in

https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/cluster-administration/networking/ , you already have a diagram there with the 3 conceptual networks, the nodes, pods and services ...

> it does require, Services is part of Conformance

Yes, if you want to sell a conformant K8s platform. But the slogan on github is:

> Production-Grade Container Scheduling and Management

And I have heard about installations where K8s is used for SW-management only. (but I haven't actually seen it I admit)

Is not about selling, the project defines APIs and behaviors, that is why e2e tests are so important, those are the ones that explain and assert how the APIs behave, so the platforms have consistency ...

Services is an integral part of the kubernetes, if people want to do custom things with pieces or strip parts of course they can, no problem at all, but all bugs are for them ;)

As @neolit123 points out in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/123120#issuecomment-1936616966, the `kubeadm` documentation is probably sufficient (nobody would probably look elsewhere).

Ref https://kubernetes.io/docs/setup/production-environment/tools/kubeadm/create-cluster-kubeadm/#network-setup

title: Kubernetes Node Resources may not have provider ID populated when using external cloud provider
body:
### What happened?

When using an external/out of band cloud providers, the responsibility of adding the provider ID to a Node resource moves from kubelet to the node controller. However because of this change, kubelet will create a node without the provider ID specified and may mark the node as ready. This has become an issue in GKE where workloads are scheduled on the node, but external networking (Ingress and Gateway) cannot proceed because the providerID is missing leading to possible downtimes every time a new node is created.

Another consequence is that if populating the [provider ID fails for any reason](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/ae185414f4e94e969399c40b23995af6f85fa37f/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L434-L437), the Node object is never updated which means information such as the zone topology and provider ID don't exist. EPS Controller uses the zone topology to populate the EPS.

### What did you expect to happen?

When using an external cloud provider, I would expect that the provider ID should gate whether the Node is considered ready or not. This would ensure that workloads are not scheduled on to a Node, until it has all relevant information populated.



### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

On any cluster that uses an external cloud provider, there will be two API calls made when a new node is created. A create call from kubelet where provider ID isn't populated and an update by the node controller.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

title: kube-proxy healthcheck all zero listening
body:
### What happened?

I have deployed a Kubernetes cluster with version 1.28 in a dual-stack environment. The main configuration for kube-proxy is as follows:
```yaml
...
--cluster-cidr=172.22.0.0/16,1111::/48
--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24
...
```
Then, I deployed a service with healthCheckNodePort: 30955 and other settings as follows:
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: my-deploy-svc
spec:
  healthCheckNodePort: 30955
  ipFamilyPolicy: PreferDualStack
  type: LoadBalancer
  externalTrafficPolicy: Local
...
```
However, port 30955 is listening on all zeros, as shown below:
```shell
tcp6       0      0 :::30955                :::*                    LISTEN      110720/kube-proxy
```
When I restarted kube-proxy, the all-zeros listening issue was resolved, and it now looks like this:
```shell
tcp        0      0 192.168.30.89:30955      0.0.0.0:*               LISTEN      25411/kube-proxy
```
I would like to know whether, in a dual-stack environment, to achieve non-all-zeros listening, both IPv4 and IPv6 address ranges must be configured for the `--nodeport-addresses` parameter. Otherwise, it may lead to the all-zeros listening issue, or it could be a kube-proxy bug. Is it related to the following code:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b1aaa5b39b351ec8586de800baa5715304a3f/pkg/proxy/metaproxier/meta_proxier.go#L55-L58
Additionally, I believe that in a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. Otherwise, the already configured IP address range may lose the non-all-zeros listening.


### What did you expect to happen?

In a dual-stack environment, if `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with one IP address range and the other IP address range is not configured, then the other IP address range cannot have all-zeros listening. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

In a dual-stack environment, `--nodeport-addresses` is configured with only one IP address range.Additionally, a Service with healthCheckNodePort is created.

/area kube-proxy
/sig network

I think, the judgment condition of the following code should be:
from:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/a07b1aaa5b39b351ec8586de800baa5715304a3f/pkg/proxy/util/nodeport_addresses.go#L53

to:
```golang
if len(npa.cidrStrings) == 0 && len(cidrStrings) == 0
```

The semantic is that an empty `--nodeport-addresses` means "open all", rather than "open nothing", so in that respect the current behavior is correct. The problem is that ipv6 "::" also includes ipv4 on Linux (but not on Windows I am told). If a fix for this is added, it should be to open "::" only for ipv6 if an ipv4 address is specified, but IMO that leads to confusion.

A _very simple_ work around is to include "::1/128" e.g. `--nodeport-addresses=192.168.30.0/24,::1/128`.
Discussed in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/114702

Thank you @uablrek 
My requirement is that in a dual-stack environment, if the --nodeport-addresses parameter is configured only with the IPv4 address range, then it should only listen on the IPv4 addresses and not have the possibility of listening on the all-zero IPv6 address. I wonder if this is reasonable?

"ugh"

(fixed in nftables! :slightly_smiling_face:)

> not have the possibility of listening on the all-zero IPv6 address

The work-around above, add "::1/128", does that. It still opens a listening port, but not exposing anything (e.g. in a port-scan).

#123105 adds `--nodeport-addresses-primary`, to tell kube-proxy to only listen on the primary node IP, and also adds a warning specifically for the case in this bug (where you have a dual-stack cluster, but are passing a single-stack `--nodeport-addresses` value).
/triage accepted

nodes.title: Add `--nodeport-addresses primary`, warn on empty `--nodeport-addresses`
nodes.body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
1. Adds `kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses primary`, which tells kube-proxy to only listen for NodePort connections (and HealthCheckNodePort connections) on the node's primary IP(s)
2. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass no `--nodeport-addresses`
3. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass a single-stack `--nodeport-addresses` but appear to have a dual-stack cluster.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #122899
Fixes #111863
(In both cases, that's "fixes" in the sense of "logs a warning if you are experiencing that bug, which we can't actually fix without potentially breaking other users")

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
This ends up reverting the API-change part of #122724; that PR made `proxyutil.NodePortAddresses` implement this functionality itself, which worked when we always wanted the behavior for nftables and never for the other backends. But if we want it to be _optional_ for the other backends, it turns out to be easier to just implement it by just passing an appropriate `nodePortAddresses []string` to the constructor instead.

The first commit ("Remove an unused type...") was something I noticed while implementing this in a different way that I then changed my mind about, so it ends up being pretty much irrelevant to this PR, but :man_shrugging: 

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)
```

/priority important-longterm

title: Do not set NetworkUnavailable condition on node controller for GCE
body:
### What happened?

This pertains more for clusters running in GCP but not necessarily in a GKE environment. Clusters that using a CNI supporting overlay such as Calico, do not need explicit routes to be created on the infrastructure level, meaning that the route controller should not be necessary. 

The following snippet https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/node/node_controller.go#L456-L468 sets the `NetworkUnavailable` condition for new GCE nodes when a new node is picked up by the node controller. This condition is supposed to be removed later by the route controller in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52457842d155743f0e3fc57ade87251cca37d375/staging/src/k8s.io/cloud-provider/controllers/route/route_controller.go#L397. However, as stated above there are cases where the route controller is not needed and should not be running.

When Calico is deployed in such a way that the calico-node pods are ignoring any and all `NoSchedule` taints including the cloudprovider's `node.cloudprovider.kubernetes.io/uninitialized` taint (which we consider reasonable for a system pod such as calico), the above check creates the following race condition:  a Calico pod may start and set the node network conditions (`NetworkUnavailable` to false) before the node controller reconciles the node. After that the node controller picks up the node and sets the `NetworkUnavailable` condition to an otherwise healthy node.

Leaving aside the race condition itself, I have to ask whether the check is meaningful in the first place. AFAIK, the kubelet in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/52457842d155743f0e3fc57ade87251cca37d375/pkg/kubelet/kubelet_node_status.go#L338 ~~already sets the same condition, so I am not sure if there is any particular reason for the node controller to make the same operation.~~ Kubelet only sets the condition for `gce` provider, but clusters should already be using kubelet with cloudprovider=`external`


### What did you expect to happen?

For the node controller to not set the `NetworkUnavailable` condition unnecessarily. 

### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?

An easy way to do it with a custom CCM image is to introduce some delay in the node sync loop, enough for pods such as calico-node to start on that node.

### Anything else we need to know?

_No response_

Any idea where `trace.go:205` is located?

<details>
<summary>
search for trace.go:205 in v1.25.5
</summary>

```bash        
$ fd --glob "trace.go" 
vendor/github.com/gorilla/websocket/trace.go
vendor/go.etcd.io/etcd/pkg/v3/traceutil/trace.go
vendor/go.opencensus.io/plugin/ochttp/trace.go
vendor/go.opencensus.io/trace/trace.go
vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/internal/global/trace.go
vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/semconv/trace.go
vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace/trace.go
vendor/go.opentelemetry.io/otel/trace.go
vendor/golang.org/x/net/trace/trace.go
vendor/google.golang.org/grpc/trace.go
vendor/k8s.io/utils/trace/trace.go
```
</details>
These are pretty critical, these trace logs are latency based, so they only trigger when you have really slow requests which signal that something is going wrong.

In absolute terms - yes.

But really we have generic log rate-limiting rules, and this results in logs from APIServer not being forwarded to aggregator and getting "dropped" by forwarders. We are pursuing this issue with Kyverno separately about their excessive use of API / ETCD.

In the meantime there is no mechanism to suppress this behaviour. I would even be happy with a grep pipe to remove, but k8s images don't have shell.

Thinking out loud - if this is an important message we want to output, can it be suppressed into "<message> and 886 messages like it in the last minute". Each individual trace doesn't carry large amount of value when they are all caused by the same client calling same functions.

Thank you.

I'd like to revive this discussion since I ran into that recently and can't really understand why we skip log levels here.

> These are pretty critical, these trace logs are latency based, so they only trigger when you have really slow requests which signal that something is going wrong.

@logicalhan slowness can for sure indicate that something is going wrong, but this is a debug information at best. I don't really understand why it is critical to the point that it skips all log levels. In most cases this will be noisy with v=0 and hide all the critical information that are present in the logs with that level set.

If we go according to our [logging conventions](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-instrumentation/logging.md#what-method-to-use), it should be level 5 or higher, but I could see them useful at the level 4 since they are key debugging information in case of slowness.

FWIW, there was an effort long ago to move all nested traces to level 4 and higher (https://github.com/kubernetes/utils/pull/177) and I think we should generalize that to all the steps that are above threshold.

Still an issue with lastest 1.28 releases. ([Slack thread](https://kubernetes.slack.com/archives/C2P1JHS2E/p1701132279167519))

Is there any kind of expected 'next action' for fixing this?

>  and I think we should generalize that to all the steps that are above threshold.

I have seen many cases where these messages in `--v=2` mode led to diagnosis of problems. I consider these trace messages (above the threshold) as warnings of something wrong. In other words: I would not be happy to move them above `--v=2`, but would be totally on-board to disable the output below.
Log level 2 sounds fine by me :+1:

title: Service NodePorts can be accessed via LB IPs (iptables, at least)
body:
Create a single-port Service of type LB.  It gets nodeport 31234.

Wait for an LB IP to be assigned.

Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.

This is because the NodPorts chain doesn't necessarily check IPs (hence why it is the last chain).  It finds port 31234 and forwards it to the Service.

I think we need to add rules to "KUBE-PROXY-FIREWALL" to allow valid IP+port combos and then drop other uses of those IPs.  Or something.

@danwinship since you are elbow-deep in that area.

This problem does not exist for proxy-mode=ipvs.
```
vm-201 ~ # curl http://192.168.1.2:30018 > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
100   232  100   232    0     0  36907      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:-- 38666
vm-201 ~ # curl http://10.0.0.80:30018  > /dev/null
  % Total    % Received % Xferd  Average Speed   Time    Time     Time  Current
                                 Dload  Upload   Total   Spent    Left  Speed
  0     0    0     0    0     0      0      0 --:--:-- --:--:-- --:--:--     0
curl: (7) Failed to connect to 10.0.0.80 port 30018 after 2 ms: Connection refused
```
192.168.1.2 is a node address and 10.0.0.80 is a LB-address.
this one? https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/110289

So, we _can_ work around this in kube-proxy, but I believe this bug is a side effect of GCE stuff which is not part of core Kubernetes. The rule that iptables kube-proxy creates to jump to the nodeports chain is:

    -A KUBE-SERVICES -m comment --comment "kubernetes service nodeports; NOTE: this must be the last rule in this chain"
        -m addrtype --dst-type LOCAL -j KUBE-NODEPORTS

`--dst-type LOCAL` means it will only match for packets that are addressed to an IP which the routing table considers to be local (meaning either the IP is assigned to a local interface, or there is an `ip route` rule intercepting traffic for that IP and delivering it to a local interface). Neither iptables kube-proxy nor the GCP CloudProvider adds LB IPs as local IPs, or adds routes directing LB IP traffic to the local host, so this rule _should not match_ LB IP traffic unless something besides core Kubernetes is mucking with the routing of LB IP traffic.

I know in OpenShift-on-GCP, there _is_ a service that does special handling for LoadBalancer IPs, and I'm pretty sure it's a fork of something that runs on GCE. The behavior in OpenShift has changed over the years, and it now uses iptables rules rather than routes, but it ends up having [the same bug](https://bugzilla.redhat.com/show_bug.cgi?id=2094408) (which I had assumed GCE _didn't_ have), and my conclusion there was that we shouldn't be running that script for LB IPs that correspond to Kubernetes Services; it should only be used for LB IPs that _aren't_ being managed by kube-proxy. (Of course if there are LB IPs that are used for both kube-proxy-managed Services and for other things, then that rule wouldn't work...)

Assuming I'm right and this service does exist in GCE, we should probably document its existence and behavior better in the kube-proxy code/docs...
note: all implementations that add IP addresses to the node may be affected by this, per example, platforms that use Keepalived on nodes for ExternalIPs  or LoadBalancer IPs

Yeah, any LB implementation that is VIP-ish should have this problem - something needs to accept VIP traffic locally.

My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" `filter` rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules.  With things like `externalIPs` it's not even obvious when to put that rule, since a single externalIP could be used on multiple Services (with disjoint sets of ports).  Also, annoyingly, this speaks to the value of KUBE-MARK-DROP, since we already enumerate all service-ip-ports in `nat`.

> My fear is that we end up with 1 "ALLOW" filter rule for every service-ip-port and then final "DROP" rules, increasing the number of iptables rules

Tim mentioned briefly in the meeting that we have all these problems with bad Service defaults, and I feel like part of the answer here might be to encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar; then we can just change the `KUBE-NODEPORTS` jump rule to only match traffic on those IPs, rather than having to un-match everything else.

(Also, if people use a `--nodeport-addresses` that doesn't include 127.0.0.1 then we can also get rid of the localhost-nodeport junk.)

But even without that, we still don't need 1 rule per IP; we can just make the iptables proxy use ipsets like the ipvs proxy does... there's no real reason other than "history" for why it doesn't.

> encourage people to use `--nodeport-addresses` or something similar

eg
`klog.Warning("--nodeport-addresses not specified; NodePorts will be available on all local IPs!")`
yeah, the `Access that LB IP on 31234 - it works as long as firewalls don't stop it.`  is totally valid if the LB IP belong to the Node ... but is this new? this should be always working like this
Yes, it always worked like this, but it was never _intended_ to work like this.

If we added `--nodeport-addresses node-ip` meaning "only accept NodePort connections on the node's primary IP (of the relevant IP family)", would that work with the various cloud load balancers that actually use NodePorts? If not, would it work if we had it mean "only accept NodePort connections on IPs in `node.Status.Addresses`"? (Yes, in both cases it would imply "no NodePorts on localhost"; people who want localhost NodePorts would have to continue not using `--nodeport-addresses` or else specify the right IP/CIDR by hand.)

nodes.title: Add `--nodeport-addresses primary`, warn on empty `--nodeport-addresses`
nodes.body:
#### What this PR does / why we need it:
1. Adds `kube-proxy --nodeport-addresses primary`, which tells kube-proxy to only listen for NodePort connections (and HealthCheckNodePort connections) on the node's primary IP(s)
2. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass no `--nodeport-addresses`
3. Adds a warning at kube-proxy startup if you pass a single-stack `--nodeport-addresses` but appear to have a dual-stack cluster.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:
Fixes #122899
Fixes #111863
(In both cases, that's "fixes" in the sense of "logs a warning if you are experiencing that bug, which we can't actually fix without potentially breaking other users")

#### Special notes for your reviewer:
This ends up reverting the API-change part of #122724; that PR made `proxyutil.NodePortAddresses` implement this functionality itself, which worked when we always wanted the behavior for nftables and never for the other backends. But if we want it to be _optional_ for the other backends, it turns out to be easier to just implement it by just passing an appropriate `nodePortAddresses []string` to the constructor instead.

The first commit ("Remove an unused type...") was something I noticed while implementing this in a different way that I then changed my mind about, so it ends up being pretty much irrelevant to this PR, but :man_shrugging: 

#### Does this PR introduce a user-facing change?
```release-note
The kube-proxy nodeportAddresses / --nodeport-addresses option now
accepts the value "primary", meaning to only listen for NodePort connections
on the node's primary IPv4 and/or IPv6 address (according to the Node object).
This is strongly recommended, if you were not previously using
--nodeport-addresses, to avoid surprising behavior.

(This behavior is enabled by default with the nftables backend; you would
need to explicitly request `--nodeport-addresses 0.0.0.0/0,::/0` there to get
the traditional "listen on all interfaces" behavior.)
```

I believe I hit the same issue (postgres works through docker run, but not k8s).  The issue I hit was that huge pages were enabled, but they were not working through k8s, and Postgres wouldn't fall back properly to not using huge pages.  I think there are several possible solutions to the problem:

1.  Modify the docker image to be able to set `huge_pages = off` in /usr/share/postgresql/postgresql.conf.sample before initdb was ran (this is what I did).
2.  Turn off huge page support on the system (`vm.nr_hugepages = 0` in /etc/sysctl.conf).
3.  Fix Postgres's fallback mechanism when `huge_pages = try` is set (the default).
4.  Modify the k8s manifest to enable huge page support (https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/manage-hugepages/scheduling-hugepages/).
5.  Modify k8s to show that huge pages are not supported on the system, when they are not enabled for a specific container.

Looks like the issue here is that the file /sys/fs/cgroup/hugetlb/kubepods/hugetlb.2MB.limit_in_bytes is set to 0 in the worker nodes. This prevents PODs from allocating huge pages. Setting this limit to a higher value in the worker nodes (It would have to be done on every node) solves it.
```
echo 9223372036854771712 | sudo tee hugetlb.2MB.limit_in_bytes
```
